timeline.title: Born in Zundert
timeline.text: Vincent Willem van Gogh was born in the village of Zundert in the south of the Netherlands. His father, Theodorus, was a Protestant minister.

timeline.title: A job selling art
timeline.text: At 16 he began work at the art dealers Goupil & Cie in The Hague. His uncle, also called Vincent, helped him get the job. He spent his days around paintings and prints.

timeline.title: Sent to London
timeline.text: Goupil moved him to its London branch. He lodged in Stockwell, south London.

timeline.title: Transferred to Paris
timeline.text: In 1875 the firm sent him to its Paris branch.

timeline.title: Dismissed, then a teacher
timeline.text: About a year after the move to Paris, Goupil let him go. In April 1876 he went back to England as an unpaid supply teacher in Ramsgate, and then at a school in Isleworth.

timeline.title: Trying to become a minister
timeline.text: After six months in a bookshop in Dordrecht, he moved in with an uncle in Amsterdam to prepare for the study of theology. He failed the university entrance exam and left in 1878.

timeline.title: Preacher to the miners
timeline.text: He became a missionary in the Borinage, a poor coal-mining region of Belgium. The church dismissed him, saying he was undermining the dignity of the priesthood.

timeline.title: I will be an artist
timeline.text: Lodging with a miner's family in Cuesmes, he drew the people around him. Here, at 27, he decided to become an artist. His brother Theo, an art dealer, supported him with money and letters.

timeline.title: Art school in Brussels
timeline.text: He registered at the Royal Academy of Fine Arts in Brussels to study drawing.

timeline.title: Lessons with Mauve
timeline.text: After months drawing at his parents' home in Etten, he went to The Hague. His second cousin, the successful painter Anton Mauve, gave him lessons, though Mauve later grew cool towards him.

timeline.title: Sorrow
timeline.text: In 1882 he met Sien Hoornik and drew her in a drawing he called Sorrow. He thought it the best figure he had drawn, and wrote that he wanted to make drawings that touch people.

timeline.title: The first oil studies
timeline.text: He bought paints and painted his first oil studies, a meadow at sunset and a stretch of dunes. He wrote to Theo that painting made him extraordinarily happy, and that his long study of drawing had prepared him.

timeline.title: Alone on the moors
timeline.text: He moved to the province of Drenthe in the north of the Netherlands to paint.

timeline.title: Home to Nuenen
timeline.text: He moved in with his parents in Nuenen. He painted weavers at their looms and farm workers, in dark earth colours.

timeline.title: His father dies
timeline.text: His father Theodorus died of a heart attack.

timeline.title: The Potato Eaters
timeline.text: He finished his first major painting, a peasant family eating supper by lamplight. He wanted to show they had honestly earned their food. Critics disliked its dark colours, but it is now one of his best-known works.

timeline.title: Antwerp
timeline.text: He moved to Antwerp and in January 1886 enrolled at the Academy. A popular story says he was thrown out, but Wikipedia calls this unfounded: he was one of 17 students told to repeat a year.

timeline.title: Paris and colour
timeline.text: He moved in with Theo in Montmartre and studied at Fernand Cormon's studio. There he met newer painters, collected Japanese woodblock prints and began to work in far brighter colour.

timeline.title: Painting by the river
timeline.text: He painted outdoors at Asnières on the Seine and tried the small dots and dashes of the Pointillists. That winter he made Self-Portrait with Grey Felt Hat, one of his boldest colour experiments. In November he met Paul Gauguin.

timeline.title: To the southern sun
timeline.text: He left Paris for Arles in the south of France, looking for strong light and colour. Most of his roughly 860 oil paintings were made in the last two years of his life.

timeline.title: The Yellow House
timeline.text: He rented four rooms in a yellow house on Place Lamartine. He dreamed of making it a home where artists could live and work together.

timeline.title: Sunflowers for a friend
timeline.text: He painted sunflowers in a vase to decorate the guest room for Gauguin. He later made repetitions of these pictures himself.

timeline.title: Painting the night
timeline.text: In one month he painted a café terrace at night on the Place du Forum, standing on the spot with his easel, a starry sky over the Rhône, and the inside of an all-night café.

timeline.title: Gauguin arrives
timeline.text: After many invitations, Gauguin came to stay at the Yellow House. For about nine weeks they painted side by side, but they argued more and more.

timeline.title: A breakdown
timeline.text: After a quarrel with Gauguin, Vincent had a severe mental crisis and injured his own left ear. He later had no memory of it. He was cared for in hospital by Dr Félix Rey, and Gauguin left Arles. The exact events are not known and accounts disagree.

timeline.title: Saint-Rémy, by his own choice
timeline.text: After more attacks of illness, he chose to enter the asylum of Saint-Paul-de-Mausole. Between attacks he painted the garden, olive groves, cypresses and wheat fields. Scholars still do not agree what illness he had; ideas include epilepsy, bipolar disorder and porphyria.

timeline.title: The Starry Night
timeline.text: He painted the view east from his window just before sunrise, adding a village from his imagination. It became one of the most recognised paintings in the world.

timeline.title: First praise in print
timeline.text: The critic Albert Aurier wrote a glowing article about him in the Mercure de France, calling him a genius.

timeline.title: Shown and sold
timeline.text: He was invited to exhibit with the group Les XX in Brussels. That year the painter Anna Boch bought The Red Vineyard, the only painting known by name that he sold in his lifetime. He also painted Almond Blossom for Theo and Jo's newborn son, named Vincent after him.

timeline.title: Auvers-sur-Oise
timeline.text: He left Saint-Rémy for the village of Auvers, near Paris and Theo. Dr Paul Gachet, a doctor and amateur painter, looked after him, and Vincent painted his portrait.

timeline.title: Wheat fields under big skies
timeline.text: He painted wide wheat fields under stormy skies. People often call Wheatfield with Crows his last painting, but that is a myth: his letters show he made several works after it.

timeline.title: His death
timeline.text: Vincent died on 29 July 1890, aged 37, from a wound he had received two days before. Most accounts describe his death as suicide. Theo was with him at the end. He was buried in Auvers the next day.

timeline.title: Jo keeps the work
timeline.text: Theo died six months after Vincent. His widow, Jo van Gogh-Bonger, was left with hundreds of paintings, drawings and letters. She played a key role in making Vincent's art known.

timeline.title: The letters are published
timeline.text: Jo published Vincent's letters to Theo in three volumes. That year she also had Theo reburied beside Vincent in Auvers.

timeline.title: The Van Gogh Museum
timeline.text: The Van Gogh Museum opened in Amsterdam, founded by Theo and Jo's son Vincent Willem. It holds the largest collection of his paintings and drawings in the world.

feature.title: Where to see the paintings
feature.lead: About 2,100 of his works survive, spread across the world. Here are key paintings and a drawing, and the places that hold them today.

items.label: Sorrow
items.place: The New Art Gallery Walsall, England
items.text: A drawing of Sien Hoornik that he called the best figure he had drawn. It is part of the Garman Ryan Collection.

items.label: The Potato Eaters
items.text: His first major painting, a peasant family at supper in dark earth colours. The oil sketch for it is at the Kröller-Müller Museum.

items.label: Self-Portrait with Grey Felt Hat
items.text: Painted in Paris with short strokes of complementary colour, blue against orange and red against green.

items.label: The Yellow House (The Street)
items.text: The house on Place Lamartine in Arles where he hoped artists would live and work together.

items.label: Sunflowers
items.text: One of the sunflower paintings he made in Arles to decorate the guest room for Gauguin.

items.label: Sunflowers (repetition)
items.text: A version he painted himself after the London picture. Other Sunflowers hang in Munich, Philadelphia and Tokyo.

items.label: Café Terrace at Night
items.text: A café on the Place du Forum in Arles, painted on the spot at night, with no black paint at all.

items.label: Starry Night Over the Rhône
items.text: The night sky over the river, painted a short walk from the Yellow House. It was shown in Paris in 1889.

items.label: The Night Café
items.place: Yale University Art Gallery, New Haven, USA
items.text: The inside of the Café de la Gare in Arles, run by Joseph and Marie Ginoux.

items.label: The Bedroom
items.text: His room in the Yellow House, planned so that the colour alone would suggest rest.

items.label: The Bedroom (second version)
items.text: He painted the bedroom three times. The second is in Chicago and the third is in the Musée d'Orsay, Paris.

items.label: The Red Vineyard
items.place: Pushkin State Museum of Fine Arts, Moscow
items.text: Workers in a vineyard near Arles. It is the only painting known by name that he sold in his lifetime.

items.label: Self-Portrait with Bandaged Ear
items.text: Painted in Arles in 1889, after his breakdown. It draws on Japanese woodblock prints.

items.label: Irises
items.place: J. Paul Getty Museum, Los Angeles
items.text: Painted in 1889 at the asylum in Saint-Rémy, with bold blue and violet flowers.

items.label: The Starry Night
items.place: Museum of Modern Art, New York
items.text: The view from his window in Saint-Rémy before sunrise, with an imagined village. At MoMA since 1941.

items.label: Wheat Field with Cypresses
items.place: National Gallery, London, and The Met, New York
items.text: He painted this view of the hills near Saint-Rémy three times; London and New York each hold one.

items.label: Almond Blossom
items.text: Blossom against a blue sky, a gift for his newborn nephew. The family always kept it closest to their hearts.

items.label: The Church at Auvers
items.text: The village church of Auvers-sur-Oise, painted in June 1890, a few weeks before his death.

works.title: Letters to Theo and friends
works.text: More than 600 letters to his brother Theo, and others to his sister Wil, Anthon van Rappard and Émile Bernard, from 1872 to 1890. They explain how and why he worked.

works.title: Sorrow
works.text: A drawing of Sien Hoornik that he called the best figure he had drawn.

works.title: The Potato Eaters
works.text: His first major painting, of a peasant family at supper by lamplight.

works.title: Self-Portrait with Grey Felt Hat
works.text: One of his boldest colour experiments in Paris, made of short strokes in complementary colours.

works.title: Sunflowers
works.text: A series of sunflowers in a vase, made to decorate the Yellow House for Gauguin.

works.title: The Yellow House
works.text: The house in Arles where he rented four rooms and hoped to found a home for artists.

works.title: Café Terrace at Night
works.text: A night scene painted outdoors on the Place du Forum in Arles.

works.title: The Bedroom
works.text: His bedroom in the Yellow House, in three versions, where colour was meant to suggest rest.

works.title: The Red Vineyard
works.text: The only painting known by name that he sold in his lifetime.

works.title: Irises
works.text: A garden study from the asylum at Saint-Rémy.

works.title: Olive Trees series
works.text: At least 15 paintings of olive groves, made at different times of day and in different seasons.

works.title: The Starry Night
works.text: The view from his window at Saint-Rémy before sunrise, with an imagined village.

works.title: Almond Blossom
works.text: Blossom branches against a blue sky, painted for his newborn nephew.

works.title: Wheatfield with Crows
works.text: A wheat field under a stormy sky from his last weeks in Auvers. It was not his last painting, despite the popular story.
